title: Momoweta
summary: Momoweta was a Corchaug sachem named in the 1644 United Colonies certificate and the 1648 East Hampton agreement. North Fork land records and the name of Lake Momoweta connect his leadership with a wider eastern Long Island history.
content:
Corchaug leadership on the North Fork

Momoweta was a seventeenth-century sachem of Corchaug on Long Island’s North Fork. His name appears as Moughmaitow in the 1644 United Colonies certificate and in several other spellings in land records. The 1648 East Hampton agreement places him alongside Wyandanch, Poggatacut, and Nowedonah.1 2

These records connect Corchaug leadership with negotiations across the eastern island and Long Island Sound. They preserve particular acts of diplomacy, rather than the dates of his birth and death.1 2

September 1644: named in a regional agreement

The United Colonies commissioners at Hartford issued a certificate naming Youghco, Wiantause, Moughmaitow, and Weenagaminin. It acknowledged their declared friendship with English and Dutch settlers while placing obligations on the leaders concerning tribute and injuries attributed to their people.1

Youghco requested the certificate and is the leader recorded as present. Momoweta’s inclusion demonstrates his place in the arrangement; the record does not say that he personally attended Hartford.1

April 29, 1648: East Hampton and continuing Native uses

The East Hampton agreement names Momoweta of Corchaug among four Native leaders dealing with Theophilus Eaton and Edward Hopkins. Its description reached from the Southampton boundary toward Napeague. The transaction brought leaders from several eastern communities into one written instrument.2

The Native parties retained hunting and fishing, shell gathering for wampum, and a share of stranded whales. Cockenoe was appointed interpreter. These clauses show the importance of continued work and access in a landscape that English buyers described as a purchase.2

May 1648: Hashamomuk and the eastern North Fork

A separate May 1648 deed identifies Mammawetough as the Corchaug sachem involved in conveying Hashamomuk and the eastern North Fork to New Haven purchasers. Tooker’s account describes the tract east of Pipe’s Neck Creek, including Oyster Ponds and Plum Island. The names locate the transaction in the connected creeks, necks, and islands of the North Fork.4

Tooker speculated that Cockenoe may also have assisted, but acknowledged that his name was absent from the surviving copy. The Corchaug deed and the East Hampton deed should therefore be read as distinct transactions, with different documentary records.4

A name in the present landscape

In his 1911 place-name study, Tooker recorded Lake Momoweta at Mattituck as named for the Corchaug sachem. The name links a familiar North Fork landscape with a person whose leadership appears in the region’s earliest colonial agreements.3 1 2

Following those connections leads from the lake and Corchaug homeland to East Hampton, Shelter Island, and Hartford. Momoweta belongs in that regional story as a named leader, alongside the better-known Wyandanch.3 1 2

References

  1. United Colonies records: Wyandanch diplomacy, 1644–1657. David Pulsifer, ed., Records of the Colony of New Plymouth, vols. IX–X (1859): IX, pp. 18–19 (1644 certificate); X, pp. 9–11 (Ninigret’s 1653 answers), 96–98 (1653 Montauk conflict), 125–134 (1654 intervention), 169–172 (1656 hearing).
  2. East Hampton records: Wyandanch agreements and canoe case. Records of the Town of East-Hampton, vol. I (1887), pp. 2–3 (1648 purchase), 172–175 (August 1660 indenture and counterbond), 198 (December 1, 1662 statement), 199–200 (January 14, 1662/63 beach agreement).
  3. Momoweta and North Fork place names. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island (1911), entry 209, pp. 139–140 (Momoweta); entry for Oyster Ponds and the May 1648 deed.
  4. Cockenoe-de-Long Island: documentary biography. William Wallace Tooker, John Eliot’s First Indian Teacher and Interpreter, Cockenoe-de-Long Island (1896): Eliot letters and the author’s identification; dated records of 1648, 1652, 1657–1659, 1667, 1669–1670, 1675, 1677, 1682, and 1687; notes 9–10, 20–25, 34–45, 70–82.
why_this_matters: Momoweta shows Corchaug leadership as active and diplomatic in the colonial record, while also revealing how much of Native leadership survives only through documents written by colonial authorities.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
